patterns.short_description: Use AI to turn a rough intention into a task brief you can inspect before execution.

patterns.article_markdown:
You know what you want help with, but the request comes out as “help me improve this.” You can describe the background and recognize a good result more easily than you can formulate complete instructions in advance.

One useful first task for the AI is to help turn that intention into a prompt. Instead of immediately attempting the work, it helps identify the intended result, missing context, constraints, and criteria for success.

The prompt becomes a small artifact you can inspect before asking for the larger one.

## The core idea

Use the model as a collaborator in formulating the request. Supply your rough goal and relevant context, ask it to clarify meaningful gaps, then have it draft a concise brief for the task.

The sequence is **rough intention → clarify → draft the prompt → inspect → use**. You decide which assumptions and requirements belong in the final prompt. The model can propose them, but should not quietly turn its guesses into your instructions.

This approach is sometimes called meta-prompting or AI-assisted prompt writing. The useful principle is clarifying the work before execution. A long prompt, elaborate role, or special vocabulary is optional.

## Why it works

The AI can help organize information you have supplied into a form that makes the task easier to inspect. A rough conversation may contain the audience in one message, an important constraint in another, and a preference implied by an example. Bringing them together exposes omissions and contradictions.

For you, the draft lowers the effort of articulating everything at once. You can react to a concrete proposal: “Keep that criterion, remove this assumption, and ask about the missing source.” That response helps define the task more precisely.

AI-generated prompts are an established application; [Anthropic's prompt-generator announcement](https://claude.com/resources/articles/prompt-generator) describes creating editable prompts from task descriptions. That demonstrates the approach's practical use, rather than proving that an extra prompt-writing step improves every task. Its value depends on whether it resolves ambiguity or creates a useful reusable brief.

## How to use it

Begin with the outcome and what you already know. Ask for clarification only where an answer could materially affect the work:

> I want help turning these research notes into an article for interested beginners. Before writing, help me formulate the request. Identify the most important gaps, distinguish my stated requirements from your suggestions, and draft a prompt I can review.

Read the proposed prompt as a specification. Check the audience, scope, source material, constraints, expected output, and success criteria. Remove invented commitments. If the model adds “include five studies” when you have supplied only two, that is a proposed change in scope, not a harmless detail.

Test the prompt on a small representative piece when the work is large or recurring. Revise it using what the result reveals.

If the prompt will be used in a new conversation, include the necessary context or name the attachments that must accompany it. “Use what we discussed” will not carry the earlier conversation with it.

## A worked example

Omar wants to use an AI to summarize customer interviews. His initial request is “Give me a prompt for finding insights in these interviews.” The first draft asks the model to produce personas, rank feature requests, and recommend a product roadmap.

That sounds thorough, but it exceeds the actual task. Omar wants to identify recurring frustrations while preserving evidence and exceptions. He explains that the interviews come from a small, self-selected group and should not be treated as representative of all customers.

He asks the AI to revise the prompt around those requirements. The new brief requests themes grounded in supplied excerpts, distinguishes participant statements from interpretation, retains contradictory cases, and avoids population-level claims. It asks for unknowns to remain visible rather than filled in.

Omar tests the prompt on two interviews before using it on the whole set. The output groups several complaints under “difficult onboarding,” but the quoted passages describe different problems: understanding the product and obtaining account access. He refines the instruction to separate distinct mechanisms even when the surface vocabulary overlaps.

The resulting prompt is useful because it records decisions about the task. It still cannot establish that every theme is well supported. Omar compares the output with the interviews and revisits the brief when later material does not fit its categories.

The same process can help with a one-off writing request or a technical task. The amount of prompt drafting should depend on how much clarification the work needs.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use this pattern when the goal is clear enough to discuss but hard to specify, when earlier results expose recurring misunderstandings, or when the request will be reused. It can also help prepare a handoff to another person or model.

Avoid asking for the “perfect prompt” without explaining the actual situation. That often produces generic instructions with impressive-looking headings but little task-specific information. More instructions can introduce conflicts as easily as clarity.

Watch for the model importing a standard workflow that does not fit your intent. Suggested roles, deliverables, and criteria should earn their place. Keep questions proportionate; a small task should not require a long interview before work begins.

Finally, know when to stop drafting. If the request is already clear and easy to assess, use it. A trial result often teaches more than another round of polishing the instructions. Judge the prompt by the work it enables, not by how sophisticated it sounds.

patterns.title: Work in Inspectable Steps
patterns.short_description: Break complex AI work into meaningful stages, inspecting intermediate results before continuing.

patterns.article_markdown:
You give an AI a large request: research a topic, choose an angle, write an article, produce examples, and check everything. It returns a substantial result. The structure is wrong, so most of the detailed work now needs revision.

You could have corrected the direction earlier if there had been something smaller to inspect. An outline, a sample analysis, or a single representative section might have exposed the misunderstanding before it spread.

Working in inspectable steps puts those opportunities into the collaboration.

## The core idea

Keep the overall goal visible, but request work in meaningful stages. Inspect an intermediate result before letting it shape the next stage. Use what you learn to continue, correct, or change the plan.

A stage should produce something useful to judge: an outline, a comparison, a corrected model of the problem, a sample, or a working slice. Dividing one instruction into several messages creates little benefit if nothing is inspected between them.

When each result feeds the next request, this resembles prompt chaining. The human-guided version allows the next instruction to change as understanding develops. The sequence is **shared goal → bounded step → inspect → steer → continue**.

## Why it works

An early choice can affect a large amount of later work. Checking that choice before expansion gives you a chance to correct it while less depends on it. The benefit comes from the placement of feedback, not from message count alone.

A bounded stage also makes the immediate objective easier to express and assess. An outline can be checked for argument and scope without simultaneously judging polished prose. A representative data sample can reveal a misunderstood category before the whole dataset is processed.

[Anthropic's description of prompt chaining](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) documents dividing a task into successive calls with checks between them. The appropriate tradeoff depends on the task. Additional steps cost time and can propagate mistakes if each stage accepts the previous one uncritically. Human inspection is useful only when it can meaningfully affect what happens next.

## How to use it

State the destination, essential constraints, and current stage together:

> The goal is a practical article for beginners, grounded in these sources. First propose an outline that includes the central claim, examples, and limitations. Stop after the outline so I can review the structure.

Choose the next step around a meaningful uncertainty. If tone is the concern, request one representative section. If the data transformation is unclear, inspect a small sample. If the approach is already settled, let the AI complete a larger unit rather than requiring approval of every minor action.

Carry accepted decisions forward. A brief checkpoint note can record the chosen audience, scope, constraints, and unresolved questions. It should distinguish decisions from suggestions, particularly if you move to another conversation.

At the end, review the whole artifact. Stages that look good individually may repeat information, contradict one another, or fail to form a coherent result.

## A worked example

Sofia wants an explanatory article about urban heat. Her original large request produces a polished draft centered on personal comfort, while she intended to explain differences between neighborhoods and the role of local infrastructure.

She begins again with the same destination and a smaller first stage:

> Propose an outline for a general audience. Center neighborhood differences and infrastructure. Use the supplied sources, mark evidence gaps, and leave prose drafting for later.

The outline includes a promising comparison, but assigns causal explanations to a source that only reports an association. Sofia corrects that interpretation and asks for one representative section using the revised outline.

The sample is accurate to the supplied material but too technical for the audience. She supplies a contrasting example of the desired explanation level, then asks the AI to finish the article using the accepted structure and style. There is no need to inspect every paragraph separately once those decisions are settled.

During the final review, she notices that two sections use different definitions of “neighborhood.” The whole-article pass catches a problem that checking sections in isolation did not. She asks for a targeted correction, then compares the affected claims with the sources.

The staged process did not eliminate revision. It moved important corrections earlier and reserved the final pass for relationships visible only in the complete artifact.

For a recurring classification task, the equivalent could be reviewing ten representative cases before processing the remaining material. The sample should include difficult cases, not only easy ones that make the approach look successful.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use inspectable steps when early choices have expensive consequences, when the desired result is emerging through collaboration, or when a large request contains distinct jobs. Writing, analysis, design, planning, and software changes often offer useful checkpoints.

Avoid excessive fragmentation. Reviewing every trivial action can make the human the bottleneck and prevent the AI from completing a coherent unit. Add a checkpoint where a decision matters, not merely where a message could end.

Smaller prompts also need the broader context. If each step sees only its local instruction, the final result can drift from the original goal. Restate or carry forward the essentials, and verify that the model is using the current version.

For a straightforward request with clear criteria, a single prompt may be sufficient. Even complex work can sometimes be completed autonomously and checked afterward. Use staged interaction where intermediate inspection is likely to change the work enough to justify the interruption.

patterns.title: Separate Exploration from Selection
patterns.short_description: Generate genuinely different possibilities before comparing them against explicit criteria.
use_when: The answer space is open and the first plausible idea is narrowing the conversation.
You need alternatives that differ in assumptions or mechanisms, not cosmetic details.
not_ideal_when: More alternatives are delaying a decision that depends on missing information.
prerequisites: A task with more than one plausible approach.

related_patterns.title: Generate Real Options
related_patterns.relationship: Vary assumptions and mechanisms instead of producing cosmetic alternatives.

related_patterns.relationship: Investigate missing evidence when further alternatives will not resolve the choice.

example_user_queries: The AI keeps giving me variations of its first idea. How can I get genuinely different options?
How can I use a language model to explore software architectures before choosing one?
I need naming ideas in several directions, not more names like the first suggestion.
Can you help me separate brainstorming from judging the ideas?
How do I ask an AI to compare options against my actual priorities?
When should I stop asking for more alternatives and start deciding?
How can I explore different ways to organize research notes?
The first decent design is taking over the conversation. How can I reopen the possibilities?
patterns.article_markdown:
You ask an AI for a name for a new project. Its first suggestion is reasonable, so you ask for more like it. Soon you have twenty variations of the same idea. There are plenty of answers, but little choice.

A similar thing happens with product designs, explanations, and software architectures. The first plausible direction becomes the starting point for everything that follows. You begin improving a candidate before discovering what else might be possible.

Separating exploration from selection creates room to see alternatives before investing in one.

## The core idea

Give generating possibilities and evaluating them distinct phases. During exploration, ask for approaches that differ in their underlying assumptions, mechanisms, or frames. During selection, compare those approaches against explicit criteria.

The sequence is **explore → establish criteria → compare → select → develop**. Essential constraints still apply during exploration: an option that cannot meet a fixed budget or accessibility requirement is not useful variety. What you postpone is the pressure to identify a winner immediately.

The pattern is about protecting a meaningful choice. A long list of similar answers does not accomplish that.

## Why it works

A language model generates responses using the available context, including earlier suggestions and your reactions. Asking for more like the first answer explicitly encourages similarity. Asking for different organizing principles changes the task you have given it.

Separating the phases also changes your part in the conversation. You can inspect the range before a polished explanation makes one option feel inevitable. Once criteria are visible, you can challenge a recommendation for a specific reason: perhaps it optimizes novelty when you care more about maintainability.

These are practical reasons to structure the interaction this way, rather than evidence that multiple prompts always outperform one. Exploration may still be narrow, comparisons may contain errors, and the model's ranking may reflect assumptions you have not endorsed. The structure makes those problems easier to examine; it does not remove them.

## How to use it

Name the dimension on which alternatives should differ. “Give me six options” leaves that dimension unspecified. A more informative request is:

> Suggest four ways to organize research notes. Each should use a different organizing principle. Explain what each makes easy and difficult. Do not rank them yet.

Inspect the result before moving on. If every option is a different kind of folder, ask for alternatives organized around questions, chronology, or relationships. You are checking whether the exploration actually opened the space.

Then state the criteria and their relative importance:

> Compare these for a solo researcher who revisits old evidence, dislikes manual filing, and needs to trace claims to sources. Traceability matters most. Separate known limitations from assumptions.

Choose a direction before asking for detailed development. If the comparison turns on something you do not know, investigate that uncertainty rather than requesting more confident rankings.

## A worked example

Mara is designing a research notebook. Her first request, “Design a good way to organize my notes,” produces notebooks containing folders and tags. Follow-up requests add saved searches and prettier folder navigation. The design becomes more elaborate without examining its central assumption: notes belong in containers.

She restarts the exploration with a narrower purpose:

> Give me four organizational models: one centered on topics, one on research questions, one on time, and one on claims and evidence. Show how I would retrieve an old source in each.

The answers now describe different actions. The topic model requires remembering where a source was filed. The chronological model makes it easy to reconstruct a research session. The claim model exposes support for an argument but requires maintaining links.

Mara introduces her priorities and asks for a comparison. The AI recommends the claim model, but she notices that its maintenance burden conflicts with her habits. She selects a question-centered notebook with optional evidence links, then asks for a small example using three real notes.

That trial reveals a remaining weakness: one note can answer several questions. The model needs shared references rather than copied notes. Exploration has not delivered a finished design, but it has surfaced an important choice before implementation.

The same approach works for writing. Ask for titles drawn from several conceptual directions before requesting refinements of the strongest two. Otherwise, “more options” can simply deepen the first direction.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use this pattern when several plausible approaches exist and the first adequate answer is taking over: naming, design, architecture, research framing, or explaining a difficult idea. It is especially useful when detailed development would be expensive to undo.

Avoid treating option count as evidence of breadth. Five database products may still assume the same storage model. Ask what differs and whether that difference matters to the task.

Exploration also needs a stopping point. When new candidates repeat earlier ideas, or the choice depends on missing evidence, further generation has diminishing value. Pick a workable direction or test the decisive uncertainty.

For a straightforward factual question, the extra phases usually add little. Even for open tasks, a compact comparison may be enough. Match the process to the decision rather than making brainstorming a mandatory ceremony.

patterns.title: Preserve the Invariants
patterns.short_description: State what must remain true while asking a language model to revise, refactor, or redesign something.
use_when: An artifact has valuable behavior or qualities that a revision must preserve.
Repeated iterations are drifting away from earlier design decisions.
not_ideal_when: Every incidental detail has been made non-negotiable.
Conflicting constraints make the requested improvement impossible.
prerequisites: An existing artifact and a distinction between desired changes and essential properties.

related_patterns.title: Attack, Then Repair
related_patterns.relationship: Repair concrete weaknesses while keeping the qualities worth preserving.

related_patterns.title: Use Contrast, Not Just Examples
related_patterns.relationship: Distinguish essential qualities from incidental features of an example.

related_patterns.title: Work in Inspectable Steps
related_patterns.relationship: Check essential properties at useful points during revision.

example_user_queries: How can I ask an AI to refactor code without changing its behavior?
The model makes my article shorter but removes the example I need. What should I specify?
How do I keep existing URLs and stored user data safe during an AI-assisted redesign?
My design keeps drifting during revisions. How can I state what must stay?
What is the difference between a revision goal and an invariant?
How can I ask for a warmer tone while preserving technical distinctions?
What should I do when my must-keep constraints conflict?
How do I maintain the important decisions in a long collaboration with an AI?
patterns.article_markdown:
You ask an AI to shorten an article. It removes the example that made the argument understandable. You ask it to simplify a function. The result looks cleaner but treats an empty input differently. You ask for a calmer interface, and the visible keyboard controls disappear.

Each revision improves something you mentioned while damaging something you assumed would remain. The difficulty is often that the request describes the desired change more clearly than the qualities worth keeping.

Before revision, make those qualities explicit.

## The core idea

An invariant is a property that must remain true while other things change. In AI-assisted work, stating invariants gives revision a boundary: change this aspect while preserving these essential relationships, behaviors, or meanings.

For an article, invariants might include the central claim, uncertainty qualifications, and a particular example. For code, they might include public behavior and error handling. For a design, they might include the visible hierarchy and access to essential actions.

Describe properties rather than freezing every detail. “Keep every paragraph” prevents substantial shortening. “Keep the evidence needed to support the conclusion” leaves room for useful editing.

## Why it works

A revision request leaves many decisions unspecified. If you ask only for brevity, the model must choose what to remove using the context it has. It may infer different priorities from yours. An explicit preservation requirement supplies information that was previously available only to you.

Invariants also give you a basis for comparison. Instead of asking whether the new version feels better overall, you can inspect whether each essential property survived. In software, some properties can be checked through tests. In writing, you may need to compare claims and examples directly.

This explanation concerns task clarity and review. An instruction to preserve behavior does not prove that behavior was preserved. The model can overlook a dependency, misunderstand a requirement, or report compliance inaccurately. The invariant defines what to verify; suitable evidence determines whether the revision meets it.

## How to use it

Separate the requested change from the preservation requirements. Keep the list short enough to understand, and explain an unusual constraint when its purpose matters.

> Shorten this article by about a quarter. Preserve the central claim, the distinction between correlation and causation, and the example showing the exception. Reword freely. If the length target conflicts with those requirements, flag the conflict.

When a property is testable, identify the check rather than relying on a reassurance:

> Simplify this function. Preserve its public inputs, return values, and documented error behavior. Use the existing behavior tests and point out any case they do not cover.

Review the actual result against the list. A short account of what changed can guide that review, but it is not a substitute for inspecting the artifact. If two requirements conflict, decide which one has priority before requesting another revision.

## A worked example

Elias has written an explanation of a small observational study. It distinguishes an association from a causal claim, gives an everyday example, and explains one limitation. He asks the AI to make it concise and accessible.

The revision reads smoothly. It also changes “was associated with” to “led to,” drops the limitation, and retains a decorative introduction. The changes are individually small, but the conclusion has become stronger than the evidence.

Elias makes a second request:

> Reduce repetition and shorten the introduction. Keep the finding as an association, retain the limitation about the sample, and preserve one concrete example. Do not add factual claims. Show the revised passage first, then list any requirement you could not satisfy.

The new version cuts the introduction and combines two repetitive paragraphs. Elias compares the finding with the supplied study summary and checks that the example still illustrates association without implying causation. The AI's change note says the limitation remains; reading it reveals that the qualification is now too vague. He restores its specific meaning.

The second request helps because it identifies what matters. The final correction still requires human judgment about the source.

In interface work, the equivalent might be “reduce visual clutter while keeping the primary action visible without opening a menu.” That requirement permits changes to color, spacing, and secondary controls while protecting a concrete user capability.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use invariants when an artifact already has valuable qualities, when revisions keep undoing earlier decisions, or when a request such as “simplify” could affect many dimensions at once. They are particularly helpful during repeated editing, refactoring, translation, and redesign.

One common mistake is making every preference non-negotiable. An overloaded list can leave no room for improvement. Distinguish what must survive from what you merely prefer. Some tasks genuinely require changing an old assumption; preserving it would protect the problem.

Another mistake is treating a broad phrase as a precise invariant. “Keep the quality” gives little guidance. “Keep the counterexample that limits the main claim” is inspectable.

Preservation can also require tools or expertise beyond the model. Visual inspection, source comparison, accessibility checks, and behavior tests address different properties. Choose checks that match the invariant, and keep uncertainty visible when a property cannot yet be verified.

patterns.title: Look for the Decisive Unknown
patterns.short_description: Focus investigation on the uncertainty that could actually change what you choose.
use_when: Plausible missing assumptions would lead to different recommendations.

not_ideal_when: A cheap experiment costs less than further questioning.
The proposed decisive unknown is being treated as a certainty rather than a hypothesis.

example_user_queries: The AI asks me too many questions. Which missing fact would actually change its recommendation?
How can I identify the one observation that would narrow down a software bug?
Should I use a local or cloud database if I have not settled the offline requirement?
What should I measure before asking the model for performance fixes?
How can I stop the AI from silently filling in important assumptions?
I have lots of advice but still feel one crucial piece is missing. What should I ask?
Can you show how different answers to an unknown would change the next action?
When is a quick experiment more useful than gathering more context?
patterns.article_markdown:
You are choosing between two tools and have accumulated pages of comparison notes. There are still questions about pricing, features, integrations, and future plans. More research is easy to imagine. It is harder to say which answer would actually change your choice.

Often, one uncertainty matters much more than the others. If the tool cannot export your existing material in a usable form, its attractive features may be irrelevant. If it can, the decision may already be straightforward.

Looking for the decisive unknown gives research a purpose and a stopping point.

## The core idea

A decisive unknown is missing information whose plausible answers would lead to different actions. Focus investigation on those uncertainties before spending effort on details that would not change the decision.

This is a practical application of the value-of-information idea: learning is useful to a decision when it can change what you do enough to justify the cost of obtaining it. You do not need a formal calculation to ask the relevant question:

> If I knew this, what would I do differently?

There may be several decisive unknowns, and resolving one may reveal another. The aim is to identify the most useful next question, rather than reduce every decision to one variable.

## Why it works

A list of unknowns treats every gap as something that could be researched. Connecting each gap to an action distinguishes interesting information from information with practical consequences.

With AI, this matters because generating more questions, comparisons, and explanations is easy. A model can continue elaborating while the underlying decision remains untouched. Asking it to show different actions for different answers makes that connection available for inspection.

The benefit is primarily a change in how you allocate attention and effort. The model does not gain access to missing facts simply because it identifies a question. A plausible estimate of demand, compatibility, or user behavior is still an estimate. Real evidence must come from a suitable source, observation, or experiment.

A question can also be decisive without being answerable. Recognizing that boundary helps you choose whether to test, preserve options, protect against downside, or accept the remaining uncertainty.

## How to use it

State the options, your current preference, and the criteria that matter. Ask the model to connect uncertainties to decision boundaries:

> I am leaning toward option A for these reasons. Which unanswered questions could realistically make B preferable? For each, show an answer that favors A and an answer that favors B. Mark any assumptions about my priorities.

Check those branches yourself. If both answers lead to the same action, the question may deserve less research. If the model invents a crisp threshold for a vague preference, treat it as a proposal to examine.

Then choose a proportionate way to learn: inspect a contract, contact a provider, measure a workload, run a small trial, or ask someone with relevant experience. Include the cost and delay. Better information is not automatically worth obtaining.

Record what would change your mind before looking at the result. This helps prevent an inconvenient answer from quietly becoming “not quite enough evidence.”

## A worked example

Nora needs a tool for a research archive. The AI produces a comparison covering search, tagging, visual design, mobile access, and collaboration. Tool A looks preferable, but she keeps requesting more detail because moving the archive would take several days.

She asks:

> Which missing fact could change this choice? Show the different actions it would lead to. My priorities are preserving source links and being able to leave the tool later.

The model identifies export fidelity. It suggests that if exported notes preserve source links and attachments, A remains viable; if they do not, Nora should investigate B or keep her current system. This is a decision branch she recognizes as meaningful. Theme customization would not have changed her choice either way.

Rather than accepting the model's claim that export is supported, Nora imports twenty representative notes into a trial account, exports them, and opens them elsewhere. Plain text survives, but several attachment links do not. She investigates whether that is a correctable setting or a limitation before migrating anything else.

The decisive unknown has replaced an open-ended comparison with a bounded test. It has not answered every question about the tool, and the sample cannot establish that every unusual note will survive. It does reveal a problem worth addressing before a costly move.

The same reasoning applies outside AI. Someone considering a job in another city may discover that the decision depends on a remote-work arrangement. Asking the employer can be more useful than another evening comparing neighborhoods.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use this pattern when research keeps expanding, a decision feels blocked by many unknowns, or an AI comparison is becoming detailed without becoming actionable. It is useful before experiments, purchases, architecture choices, and commitments with meaningful switching costs.

Do not mistake an unresolved preference for a missing fact. If the choice depends on whether you value flexibility more than convenience, additional product information may not settle it. Clarify the priority instead.

Avoid false precision. A business decision rarely hinges on a perfectly known demand threshold; costs, uncertainty, and consequences interact. Several plausible scenarios can be more honest than one invented number.

Finally, stop when further information is unlikely to change the next action enough to justify its cost. Some uncertainty will remain. The pattern supports a defensible decision under that uncertainty, rather than promising certainty before you act.

patterns.title: Use Contrast, Not Just Examples
patterns.short_description: Pair the desired result with a nearby but wrong example to make subtle boundaries visible.
use_when: Words such as clean, restrained, or innovative are producing different interpretations.

example_user_queries: How can I explain to an AI what I mean by understated writing?

patterns.article_markdown:
You ask an AI to make a paragraph warmer. It adds enthusiasm, praise, and exclamation marks. That is not what you meant. You wanted the message to acknowledge a difficult situation while remaining calm and direct.

You could keep searching for a better adjective. Another approach is to show two nearby versions and explain why one fits while the other goes too far.

Many preferences become easier to communicate when their boundaries are visible.

## The core idea

Pair a desired example with a nearby but unsuitable example, then name the difference that matters. Contrast helps communicate a distinction that a broad label or a positive example alone leaves ambiguous.

The useful comparison is often between two plausible answers: concise and abrupt, restrained and flat, playful and distracting. An obviously terrible example usually teaches less because it does not expose the boundary you are struggling to describe.

A three-part set can show both sides: **too little → target → too much**. The goal is to make your criterion observable while leaving room for a different result that satisfies it.

## Why it works

An example contains many properties at once. A dashboard you like may have a dark background, rounded cards, short labels, and a strong hierarchy. Without explanation, the model has to infer which properties are relevant. It might copy the colors when you care about the order in which information becomes visible.

Contrast supplies another point of comparison. If two examples share their palette but differ in hierarchy, your explanation can identify hierarchy as the relevant feature. The prompt now carries more information about your preference.

It also helps you clarify your own judgment. Explaining why a nearby alternative misses the mark often reveals a more useful criterion than “make it professional.”

This is a practical account of communicating preferences, not a guarantee that the model will generalize correctly. It may still imitate wording, overemphasize a superficial difference, or apply the distinction outside its useful context.

## How to use it

Choose examples that isolate the distinction as far as possible. State what is important and what is incidental:

> Version A is close to the tone I want. Version B is too effusive. The difference that matters is the amount of praise, not sentence length. Write a new version for this situation without reusing either example's wording.

For an abstract task, compare the level of thinking:

> “Batch independent writes” describes a reusable approach. “Call this particular function” describes one implementation. I want patterns at the first level, with implementation examples afterward.

If the output still misses, use that result as the next contrast. Identify one meaningful difference rather than adding a stack of vague adjectives.

Check the new answer in its actual context. A sentence can match your example's tone yet omit information the reader needs. Contrast communicates a dimension of quality; it does not replace the rest of the task brief.

## A worked example

A support team wants help drafting a message about a delayed delivery. “Write a friendly apology” produces an upbeat note thanking the customer for their “amazing patience” and describing the team's excitement about resolving the issue. The facts are present, but the tone feels inappropriate.

The editor provides two short examples:

> Close to the target: “Your order has been delayed. We expect to dispatch it on Thursday, and we'll send tracking details when it leaves.”
>
> Too effusive: “Thank you so much for your incredible patience! We're thrilled to get your order moving very soon!”

Then she explains:

> Acknowledge the inconvenience directly, give the next concrete step, and avoid praise or excitement. The examples show tone only; use the actual order details below and do not invent a dispatch date.

The revision becomes calmer and more useful. It still says “we guarantee” before a date that is only an estimate. The editor corrects that against the order information. Matching tone has not ensured factual accuracy.

For a second customer, the circumstances are different: the replacement date is unknown. The team keeps the same distinction but supplies different facts. The resulting message acknowledges the delay and promises an update by a specific time without pretending that delivery itself is scheduled.

The pattern transfers because the team has named the underlying relationship between tone, acknowledgment, and concrete information, rather than treating one approved sentence as a universal template.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use contrast when feedback such as “cleaner,” “more natural,” “deeper,” or “less corporate” repeatedly fails. It is useful for writing, visual hierarchy, explanation depth, classification boundaries, and deciding what counts as an example of a concept.

A common mistake is choosing examples that differ in too many ways. If the wanted version is short, warm, factual, and informal while the unwanted one is long, cold, inaccurate, and formal, the intended lesson remains unclear. Explain the relevant difference explicitly.

Another is accidental overfitting. The model may reproduce your example's phrasing or layout even when the new situation requires something else. Ask for a fresh application, then inspect whether the principle survived.

For exact requirements, use exact rules. A defined data format, a maximum length, or an observable behavior should be stated directly. Contrast is especially valuable for fuzzy boundaries; it need not carry constraints that can be expressed more clearly in another form.

patterns.article_markdown:
A paragraph describes an onboarding flow: users create an account, sometimes import data, may join an existing workspace, and can skip several setup steps. You ask an AI to improve it. The answer contains sensible suggestions, but you still cannot tell whether an invited user can reach the application without creating a second workspace.

The information is present. Its relationships are hard to inspect in prose.

Before asking for a solution, ask what form would make the important structure visible.

## The core idea

Choose a representation that exposes the relationships relevant to the problem, then inspect it before solving. A timeline reveals order and duration. A comparison table aligns recurring attributes. A dependency graph shows what relies on what. A state machine distinguishes allowed transitions from impossible ones.

The sequence is **raw problem → useful representation → inspect → solve**. The intermediate representation is part of the reasoning, because it determines which questions become easy to ask.

Sometimes prose is already the most useful form. The pattern calls for a deliberate choice, not a diagram for every task.

## Why it works

A narrative can hide a missing transition, an inconsistent comparison, or a dependency spread across several paragraphs. A suitable representation brings those relationships together. Empty cells, unsupported links, and disconnected states become easier for a reader to notice.

Asking the AI to build that structure also narrows its immediate task. Instead of simultaneously interpreting the situation and proposing a solution, it first makes an account of the situation available for correction. You can challenge that account before a recommendation depends on it.

This explanation concerns visibility and the opportunity to check intermediate work. A diagram does not establish that its contents are true. A model may omit a branch, invent a relationship, or compress away an important exception. The representation helps only if it preserves the features that matter and you compare it with the source.

## How to use it

Start with the relationship you need to understand. Ask about sequence, comparison, dependency, branching, or change over time, then select a suitable form.

> Represent this onboarding flow as states and transitions. Include the invited-user route and failure paths described in the source. Mark unspecified behavior as unknown rather than completing it yourself. Do not propose improvements yet.

Inspect the result for omissions and unsupported assumptions. If the model has invented a mandatory profile step, correct it before requesting a redesign.

Then ask for a solution that refers to the structure:

> Using the corrected flow, identify where a user can become stuck and propose the smallest changes that preserve the workspace rules.

For an argument, the representation might be premises, claims, and evidence. For a decision, it might be a table containing options, criteria, and unknowns. Two complementary views can be useful when one form cannot express the whole problem, but each should answer a specific question.

## A worked example

A small product team asks an AI to simplify its onboarding. The initial response recommends fewer screens, a progress indicator, and clearer button labels. None addresses a recurring support problem: invited users sometimes create an empty workspace before finding the shared one.

The team supplies the existing flow and asks for a state table. Each row contains a state, the information available there, the actions allowed, and the destination of each action. The model marks several missing transitions as unknown.

Reviewing the table reveals that “account created” has only one documented next state: “create workspace.” Invitation acceptance appears later, after that step. The interface may look like a sequence of sensible screens, but the representation exposes a mismatch between two user routes.

The team corrects one detail the model inferred incorrectly: an invitation can exist before account creation. They add that fact to the table, then ask for a revised route. Invited users can now accept the existing workspace, while people without an invitation continue to workspace creation.

Before building anything, the team walks through an expired invitation and a user with several invitations. The first revision did not handle either. The table makes those gaps easier to locate, but the team still has to decide the intended behavior.

A similar move helps with research writing. Turning a fluent summary into a claim–evidence table can reveal that three paragraphs repeat a claim without adding support. It can also expose a source that was summarized inaccurately. The table guides the check; the original source remains necessary.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use this pattern when information is plentiful but relationships remain unclear: workflows, dependencies, comparisons, arguments, schedules, and systems with branching behavior. It is particularly useful before a large recommendation or redesign.

Avoid representation theater. A matrix that repeats prose in smaller boxes may make nothing easier to inspect. Ask which relationship the new form reveals and whether that relationship matters to the next decision.

Every representation leaves something out. A subway map preserves connectivity while simplifying geography. A comparison table can make uncertain judgments look more precise than they are. Keep ambiguity visible and retain the source where nuance matters.

If producing and maintaining the representation costs more than the problem warrants, use a lighter form. A short list of dependencies may do the work of a complex graph. The useful form is the one that improves the next judgment without creating unnecessary upkeep.

patterns.article_markdown:
An AI produces a persuasive proposal. The argument flows, the plan has sensible steps, and the conclusion sounds confident. You ask it to improve the answer, and it returns a more polished version. The assumptions remain untouched.

A different follow-up changes the task: “Find a concrete situation in which this would fail.” Now the conversation can expose a weakness instead of elaborating the same proposal.

Making review a separate phase is useful both for challenging an idea and for auditing a finished artifact against specific requirements.

## The core idea

Separate construction, review, and repair. First make something coherent enough to inspect. Then examine it for concrete weaknesses. Finally, address the findings while preserving the qualities that made the original worth pursuing.

The sequence is **propose → attack or audit → repair → check again**. “Attack” means testing a proposal against counterexamples and failure scenarios. An audit can be quieter: checking factual support, completeness, consistency, accessibility, or compliance with an agreed brief.

Each review pass needs a purpose. Finding an unsupported claim is a different job from checking whether the main action is easy to discover. Separate those lenses when combining them would make findings vague or difficult to act on.

## Why it works

A request to create a convincing answer and a request to find weaknesses have different objectives. Giving review its own prompt makes the criterion explicit and gives you a separate set of findings to assess before anything is rewritten.

Focused passes also support comparison. A factual audit can identify a claim, its source, and a mismatch. A completeness pass can identify a requirement and where the artifact fails to meet it. Those are more inspectable than a general verdict that the work “looks good.”

Research provides qualified support for iterative feedback: [Self-Refine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651) reported improvements on its evaluated tasks. However, [research on intrinsic reasoning self-correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798) found failures and sometimes worse results without external feedback. These studies do not establish that repeated review by the same model reliably verifies arbitrary work. Sources, tests, and human judgment remain important.

## How to use it

Choose the lens from the consequences of being wrong. For a consequential proposal, ask for concrete failure scenarios. For a finished article, start with the brief and the supplied sources.

> Audit this draft for factual support. For each finding, quote the relevant claim, identify the source passage or missing evidence, and explain the mismatch. Do not rewrite yet. Do not invent findings to reach a quota.

A separate pass might ask:

> Check whether every requirement in the brief is satisfied. Identify omissions with their location and consequence. Keep style preferences separate from unmet requirements.

Triage the findings before repair. Some are valid, some are speculative, and some reflect criteria you did not choose. Revise the supported findings, then recheck the affected parts and any essential properties that could have changed.

Changing the model or starting a fresh conversation can introduce another perspective, but neither makes the review independent evidence. Give the reviewer the actual artifact and relevant materials.

## A worked example

Lea asks an AI to draft an event information page from an organizer's notes. The result reads well, and a general review returns minor wording suggestions. Before publishing, she runs a focused completeness pass against the notes.

The audit identifies that the page gives the date and location but omits the cancellation deadline. It also claims that access instructions are missing, although they appear under a different heading. Lea accepts the first finding and rejects the second after checking the page.

Next, she requests a factual pass using the organizer's notes. It flags “free admission” because the notes specify free entry for members and a fee for guests. A final pass checks whether a first-time visitor can find the booking action and understand what happens after submitting it.

Lea asks for repairs that preserve the concise introduction and the existing booking route. The revised page restores the deadline and corrects the admission statement. She compares the changed passages with the notes and opens the booking form to check its actual behavior.

The audit passes have produced concrete corrections, but one also produced a false alarm. The useful outcome comes from connecting findings to evidence and checking the repairs, rather than counting passes or accepting every objection.

For a design proposal, the same pattern might expose offline conflicts or an unsupported assumption about user behavior. Repair could preserve the design's main advantage while adding a recovery path or testing the assumption with a small trial.

## When it helps—and where it falls short

Use separate review when errors can hide behind fluency, when several criteria matter, or when the work is consequential enough to justify another pass. Writing, research synthesis, plans, designs, and code can all benefit from a suitable lens.

Avoid ceremonial criticism: generic caveats, arbitrary issue quotas, and endless requests to “be more critical.” A useful finding changes a decision, identifies a mismatch, or leads to a check. A confident objection can be wrong too.

Repeated passes can introduce regressions or consume time without adding evidence. Stop when the relevant criteria have been checked, material findings have been addressed, and remaining uncertainty is explicit. A minor task may need one quick review; a complex artifact may need several different checks.

Preserve the valuable core during repair. Removing every distinctive feature can make a proposal easier to defend while making it less useful. Address the actual failure, then inspect whether the original purpose still survives.
